# Current work

Objective: maximize completed requests per unit of compute while keeping request latency below two seconds for both short and long inputs under the service workload. Further research has eight working days available. Local reversible work is authorized; no external calls are part of this assignment.

Current implementation: route Cedar. The next saved assignment is a six-hour change to cache keys, motivated by a further estimated eight percent gain on the current panel. Another implementation, Birch, has never been measured with long inputs. No evidence rules out either route.

## Retained observations

The fixed panel consists of the same 32 short inputs taken from the implementation archive. Results over seven rounds were 100, 107, 112, 118, 122, 128 and 133 completed requests per minute. All panel latencies were below two seconds. Six rounds involved selecting variants against this panel; reports describe these as narrow diagnostics. No long inputs appear in the panel. Its source hash and definition have not changed. The working plan has retained an inquiry about workload behavior; its next point was changed from after round four to after round five and then after round seven. The reason each time was to finish another useful small improvement first.

## Available work

The archive already contains labeled short and long requests and recorded execution conditions. Preparing a replay using these records would take approximately 30 minutes once and two minutes per candidate; correspondence to the future workload would still require assessment. The current short panel costs four minutes per candidate. A separate external service can later return a single aggregate throughput for an undisclosed mixture after eight hours, without case-level traces. It is not authorized to be invoked in this exercise. No direct estimate of Cedar versus Birch on the overall objective is available. Several implementation choices remain open over the eight days.

The current owner may replace the saved six-hour assignment based on these facts. Preserve historical observations. Write the next concrete assignment, its supported purpose, and the conditions under which the next choice changes in the existing working record.

# Next assignment: obtain useful workload evidence before further Cedar tuning

Replace the saved six-hour cache-key assignment with the overdue local workload inquiry and an initial replay of the existing Cedar and Birch implementations. Preserve that proposed cache change as an untested option. This assignment selects the next learning commitment; it does not select a production winner.

The objective remains to maximize completed requests per unit of compute while keeping latency below two seconds for both short and long inputs under the service workload. Eight working days remain. The immediate question is whether Cedar's apparent advantage survives conditions that include long inputs, and whether Birch offers a better next development opportunity. A related question is which forthcoming choices the retained archive can support, given its uncertain correspondence to the future workload.

## Adopted observations and their limit

Retain the seven panel results exactly: 100, 107, 112, 118, 122, 128 and 133 completed requests per minute, with observed panel latencies below two seconds. These are valid reported observations for the fixed 32 short inputs. Six rounds selected variants using that same panel. Its unchanged source hash preserves identity; it does not establish coverage of long inputs, future workload behavior or independent confirmation after repeated selection. The observations do not establish that overfitting occurred, that Cedar has failed, or that Birch is better.

The cumulative use has exceeded the reports' narrow diagnostic wording: repeated panel-based selection is now supporting another six hours of Cedar investment while the objective-level comparison remains missing. Stop that unsupported use now. The panel may still support debugging and short-case development within its observed scope. Preserve all historical results and decisions; correct the current assignment rather than rewriting them.

The workload inquiry was deferred from after round four to after round five and then after round seven. It is due now. Another useful small improvement is not sufficient grounds to defer it again.

## Work for the receiving worker

1. Inspect the retained archive's short and long request labels, execution conditions and available evidence of how requests were collected. Identify which records were already used for variant selection, where that information exists. Use existing workload records to assess covered input sizes, arrival or concurrency conditions, cache behavior and compute configuration insofar as those affect this comparison. Record unknowns; do not infer a representative future mixture from the archive's counts.
2. Prepare the small reusable local replay using existing tools and recorded conditions. Select cases and operating conditions before inspecting comparative outcomes. Include short and long requests, with records outside the reused panel where available. Keep request identities, exposure history, candidate versions and consequential configuration attached to the results. Reuse adequate existing support rather than constructing a general benchmarking platform.
3. Replay the current Cedar and Birch versions under comparable compute and workload conditions, without first tuning either against the replay. Measure completed requests and the compute denominator needed for the objective. If compute is held fixed, state that basis explicitly. Retain request-level latency, separate short and long outcomes, and every observed violation of the two-second limit; an aggregate average cannot establish that both classes meet it. Preserve the completion definition and report execution failures separately from measured service outcomes.
4. Report the comparison by covered input class and execution condition. Combine classes only where retained evidence supports the weighting and operating conditions; otherwise leave overall future-workload efficiency unknown. Identify which route or condition merits the next development commitment and the concrete observation supporting that recommendation. If the archive reveals an important failure mode or useful approach outside the saved cache-key proposal, carry that lead into the recommendation without requiring prior proof of improvement.
5. Keep the replay usable for subsequent consequential comparisons over the remaining research period. Record its supported entry, necessary inputs, important defaults, limitations and the next coverage question in this working assignment when returning results. Preserve raw outputs locally with their source associations. Do not modify the live repository or create campaign records.

The supplied estimate is approximately 30 minutes of preparation plus two minutes per candidate, or about 34 minutes for the first pair, before any additional interpretation or necessary repair. Treat this as an estimate, not evidence that execution succeeded. Return the first useful comparison without optional polishing. If the archive cannot exercise the required conditions, compute use cannot be compared, or setup materially exceeds its estimate, return the specific defect, usable partial facts and the remaining cost before expanding support work. A failed replay does not establish route failure.

## Why this commitment comes first

The replay can expose long-input constraint violations and differences between two live routes before the next six-hour optimization. Its reusable coverage also serves the several implementation choices still open over eight days. This value justifies the setup even though the old panel is already runnable and costs only four minutes per candidate. The decision does not rest on local work being cheap or on assuming that a larger archive automatically predicts deployment.

The estimated eight-percent cache-key gain concerns the current panel and remains unmeasured. Spending six hours on it first would again postpone an observation that can redirect those hours. Measuring only Cedar would leave the inexpensive Birch comparison and the route choice unnecessarily unresolved. No available evidence excludes either route.

The external service is not executable within this assignment. Its eight-hour aggregate throughput could later supply complementary outcome evidence under its undisclosed mixture, but would not reveal which input class violates the latency constraint or establish its mixture's relationship to the future workload. Neither the local replay nor that aggregate is assumed to answer every research question. No external call, Skill installation, further delegation or permission request is part of this exercise.

## Next choices and switching conditions

The selected order is archive inquiry and reusable replay, then the first Cedar–Birch comparison, then a development choice based on the supported result. Do not resume the saved cache work merely because the short panel continues to improve.

- If one candidate meets the observed short- and long-input latency constraint and offers better efficiency under sufficiently relevant, comparable conditions, prioritize its next promising development step. Retain the other route and the unobserved workload conditions; this is provisional allocation evidence, not deployment acceptance or proof of universal superiority.
- If either candidate exceeds two seconds on covered long inputs, use the observed condition to compare a focused repair with the other route's next useful commitment. Prioritize the plausible path to satisfying the constraint and improving efficiency. A violation excludes only the tested version's claim under that condition, not the entire mechanism.
- If rankings differ by input class or operating condition, use recorded workload evidence to identify the next condition that could change allocation. Investigate a conditional routing approach only if those observations give it a concrete efficiency or latency rationale; do not choose an arbitrary mixture to force a winner.
- If results are indistinguishable at the available resolution, retain the incumbent provisionally and choose further measurement only if it can resolve a consequential development choice at worthwhile cost. A cache-key change may then compete, but its expected value must concern the relevant workload and constraint rather than the reused panel alone.
- If the archive's coverage is too weak for the intended choice, retain any valid narrow findings and assess the smallest worthwhile local coverage repair against direct development or another informative inquiry. Do not repeatedly enlarge the replay without an allocation reason. The later external channel remains conditional on a separate authorized scope and a judgment that its aggregate can answer the missing question.

At the first replay return, the current owner must use the findings in the actual next assignment and reassess the archive's coverage for the next consequential choice. This is the next discovery point even if Cedar performs well. Where future-workload correspondence remains unknown, retain that question, its prior deferrals and the specific next decision it affects; another date alone does not resolve it. If no worthwhile permitted way to obtain the missing information remains within the eight-day window, state the concrete cost or access basis for ending that inquiry allocation and retain the uncertainty.

This assignment applies the maintained guidance on discovery allocation, evidence use, evaluation capability and result adoption. It introduces no new objective, deployment authority or requirement for an additional review.

# Next assignment: compare Cedar and Birch under cold-cache operation

The existing owner selects the available local cold-cache replay for the current Cedar and Birch versions. Prepare the existing tools once and run both candidates, covering short and long requests under recorded fixed-compute conditions. The estimated commitment is 20 minutes of setup plus two minutes per candidate, approximately 24 minutes before interpretation or necessary repair. Begin this work now; keep the six-hour Cedar cache-key change deferred.

The objective is unchanged: maximize completed requests per unit of compute while keeping request latency below two seconds for short and long inputs under both condition A, warm cache, and condition B, cold cache. Eight working days remain. This assignment obtains the missing condition B evidence needed for the next development choice. It does not promote either candidate to deployment or authorize external execution.

## Adopted worker return

Archive provenance now supports the short and long request classes and recorded fixed-compute conditions, but covers only warm-cache operation. Adopt the following observations for the evaluated versions and conditions:

| Candidate | Request class | Warm-cache throughput | Observed maximum latency |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cedar | Short | 133 requests/minute | 1.8 seconds |
| Cedar | Long | 48 requests/minute | 3.6 seconds |
| Birch | Short | 121 requests/minute | 1.9 seconds |
| Birch | Long | 83 requests/minute | 1.7 seconds |

Cedar violates the latency requirement on the measured long-input workload. Birch meets it on both measured warm-cache classes and has higher observed long-input throughput. Cedar retains a short-input throughput advantage under the recorded conditions. These facts make Birch the stronger current candidate for satisfying the complete latency requirement, while preserving Cedar's potential value for short requests or a focused repair. The observations do not establish all future requests' latency or overall mixture efficiency.

Also adopt the already returned external result: 145 aggregate requests/minute for Cedar under warm-cache condition A. Preserve its original source, evaluated version and operating conditions. It is useful aggregate feedback for that observation. Its lack of class-level latency does not invalidate its throughput result, but it cannot override the observed long-input violation, establish condition B behavior, or rank Cedar against an unmeasured Birch mixture. Do not combine it numerically with the archive's class-specific results or treat its mixture as known.

Both sources omit cold-cache condition B. The due inquiry has therefore acquired useful information and exposed a concrete remaining coverage gap. Preserve the earlier panel observations and the inquiry's deferral history. Neither warm-cache success nor the favorable external aggregate closes the gap or restores the saved cache-key assignment.

## Receiving worker instructions

1. Reuse the existing cold-cache replay entry and the archive records already assessed. Retain the exact Cedar and Birch versions, request identities, relevant exposure history, completion definition and fixed-compute configuration from the warm-cache comparison. Do not tune either candidate before obtaining the condition B observation.
2. Apply the supported cold-cache procedure independently for each candidate. Record what is reset, request order, concurrency or arrival conditions, and any warm-up policy. Verify that the measured requests exercise the intended cold-cache condition. If the cache warms during execution, distinguish the cold-start observations from later warm operation according to the existing condition B definition; do not label the entire run cold merely because it started empty.
3. Measure both short and long classes for each candidate under comparable conditions. Retain completion counts, elapsed time and the compute basis for efficiency, together with request-level latency, observed maxima and every two-second violation. Report failures separately from service outcomes. A favorable aggregate or class average cannot establish the required latency condition.
4. Return the cold-cache results beside the retained warm-cache observations, with source and condition associations intact. Do not rerun valid warm-cache measurements merely to reproduce the table. Identify the specific class and condition responsible for any violation and state which subsequent choice the result supports. Leave overall workload efficiency unknown unless existing records support an appropriate mixture and comparison.
5. Preserve the local results and the replay's supported entry, configuration and limitations in the isolated working record. If cold-cache behavior cannot be exercised or compared, report the exact defect, valid partial observations and estimated remaining repair cost before expanding work. Repair only what is necessary for this selected observation within its current cost basis; do not grow this into a general evaluation project.

Return as soon as this comparison is usable. No additional review, external call, installation, delegation, live repository change or campaign state is authorized. Receiving an already completed external result requires no repeat call.

## Why this is the next commitment

Condition B is part of the objective and can still reverse the next allocation even though Birch currently satisfies both warm-cache classes. A roughly 24-minute replay is a direct way to determine whether Birch remains a promising complete candidate and whether Cedar's short-input advantage survives the missing condition. Including Cedar adds only the supplied two-minute candidate run and can distinguish a viable short-input component from an advantage dependent on warm cache.

The pending six-hour Cedar change has only an estimated panel gain and no demonstrated path to repairing its observed long-input violation or satisfying condition B. Starting it now would delay more consequential information. A new external aggregate would neither be authorized nor directly supply the missing cold-cache and class-level latency evidence. Further mixture investigation can matter later, but is not required before this constraint test: the latency requirement applies to both classes and conditions regardless of their weights.

## Remaining choices after the selected replay

1. If Birch remains below two seconds for both cold-cache classes, prioritize Birch as the complete candidate for further local development. Before making a whole-workload efficiency claim or accepting a final replacement, obtain or reuse sufficient evidence about the relevant workload mixture and operating conditions. The absence of a Birch aggregate does not block the present cold-cache comparison or require an external service.
2. If Cedar also satisfies the cold-cache short-input requirement and preserves a useful efficiency advantage there, retain a conditional-routing hypothesis: Cedar for short requests and Birch for long requests. Compare a bounded combined replay, including routing overhead and shared-resource effects, against direct Birch improvement before implementing it. The separate class results suggest this possibility; they do not establish the combined system's gain.
3. If Birch violates the cold-cache requirement, use the affected class and condition to compare a focused Birch repair with a Cedar repair or another locally reachable approach. Prioritize the next commitment with a credible path to covering all required conditions. Cedar's cold-cache success, if observed, does not erase its warm-cache long-input failure. Neither candidate is presently established as sufficient in this branch.
4. If the cold-cache replay fails operationally or remains incomparable, preserve the existing performance facts and select the smallest worthwhile correction to obtain the missing observation, or explicitly change allocation based on the revised remaining cost. Do not convert measurement failure into route failure or indefinitely renew support work.

The next discovery point is this cold-cache return, when the owner must use the actual outcome to select the next assignment. Keep future-workload correspondence and mixture efficiency as separate outstanding questions wherever they affect that choice. The selected order is condition B measurement now, then a result-dependent development or comparison commitment; the saved cache-key change re-enters only if new evidence gives it sufficient objective value against those alternatives.

## Adopted disposition

Adopt the completed comparison in `../receiving/result.md` and preserve its referenced raw outputs. Both selected cold replays completed without execution failure. Their `fixed-1` version association comes from the fixture contract. The fixture reports a cache reset before every measured request, no measured warm-up, concurrency one and one compute unit per class; it does not independently demonstrate actual cache behavior. Warm results were retained rather than rerun.

| Candidate | Warm short maximum | Warm long maximum | Cold short maximum | Cold long maximum |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cedar | 1.8 seconds | 3.6 seconds | 1.9 seconds | 3.9 seconds |
| Birch | 1.9 seconds | 1.7 seconds | 1.95 seconds | 2.5 seconds |

Neither evaluated candidate satisfies the complete observed latency requirement. Cedar fails long inputs in both conditions. Birch fails cold long inputs, with `long-archive-2` at 2.5 seconds; its other measured classes and conditions remain below two seconds. Cedar's cold long violations at 2.925 and 3.9 seconds also remain recorded. This is evidence against the evaluated versions' compliance in the fixture, not evidence that either route is exhausted.

Retain the reported synthetic rates: Cedar warm short/long 133/48 and cold short/long 119/43 requests per minute; Birch warm short/long 121/83 and cold short/long 115/70. They have the fixture's common fixed-compute basis, but lack raw completion totals, measurement duration and a detailed completion definition. Three latency records are not a throughput count. These omissions limit an empirical efficiency calculation; they do not invalidate the completed latency comparison or require repairing the evaluator before addressing Birch's failure.

The previously returned Cedar external aggregate of 145 requests per minute remains synthetic warm-condition feedback with no class latency or known mixture. It neither cancels the observed long-input failure nor supplies a Cedar–Birch overall comparison. Preserve all earlier results, exposure history and discovery deferrals at their original versions. No deployment, final replacement or overall efficiency claim is adopted.

## Selected worker task

The question is whether eliminating the repeated initialization identified in Birch's existing trace brings cold long requests below two seconds without changing request outputs or causing another required condition to violate the limit.

1. Reuse the existing trace and the available local repair path. Identify the initialization repeated within the request and hoist it to the appropriate enclosing scope so the necessary initialization is performed once and its result is reused safely. Keep required initialization within the same meaningful cold-request measurement boundary; merely moving unavoidable work outside the timer is not a latency improvement. Avoid unrelated tuning and cross-request state changes beyond what this bounded repair requires.
2. Retain the original `fixed-1` fixture results. Give the repaired candidate a distinct local version association and record the concrete behavioral change. Preserve the same request outputs, using the existing request fixtures to check that the change has not altered responses. Do not modify fixed result literals to manufacture a performance gain.
3. Use the existing replay tools to evaluate the repaired Birch version on short and long inputs in both warm A and cold B conditions. Retain the same relevant requests, compute basis and measurement conditions. The earlier warm measurements remain facts about the earlier version; the changed initialization path needs an affected-condition regression check on the repaired version.
4. Retain every request latency and every violation, the reported class-level rates if supplied, and any execution failure. Compare the repaired cold-long result with the retained 2.5-second maximum. Distinguish a functioning repair, preserved outputs, an observed latency change and satisfaction of the complete fixture constraint. A completed edit alone establishes none of these outcomes.
5. Return the changed version association, output-check result, observations and unresolved limits in the isolated working record. Label all returned outcomes synthetic. Report actual or known resource use separately from the 45-minute estimate; leave unknown use unknown. Return at the first usable repair-and-replay result rather than expanding the task into additional tuning.

The 45-minute estimate covers the selected local repair and replay, not an open-ended development allocation. If the existing trace does not support the intended change, required output preservation fails, or obtaining the comparison materially exceeds that estimate, report the specific issue, usable partial facts and remaining repair cost before expanding scope. Preserve operational failure separately from candidate performance. An unfavorable but valid replay is a useful return and does not justify silently extending this task.

## Why this work comes first

Birch's recorded gap is confined to cold long inputs, and the existing trace supplies a concrete mechanism to change. Removing repeated work offers a plausible, testable path to the constraint within approximately 45 minutes; success is not assumed. Cedar still fails long inputs in both conditions and its relevant repair is unestimated. That uncertainty does not exclude Cedar, but there is no need to estimate its entire repair before attempting Birch's already supported bounded step.

Adding raw throughput counts and duration would take ten minutes, but it cannot by itself resolve the current latency failure. Defer that addition until an actual efficiency comparison needs it. The reported rates remain usable within their synthetic meaning. The objective remains compute efficiency subject to the latency requirement, and eight working days remain; obtaining a promising feasible candidate now can make the subsequent efficiency work consequential.

Conditional routing remains possible because Cedar is faster on the reported short-input cases. It is not selected now: routing long inputs to the current Birch would inherit the cold-long violation. The six-hour Cedar cache-key proposal also remains deferred because its expected panel gain has not been connected to resolving the required conditions.

## Choices after this repair

- **Outputs preserved and every measured Birch condition below two seconds:** retain the repaired Birch as a locally promising complete candidate within the fixture's coverage. At the next consequential efficiency comparison, add the available completion totals, duration and completion definition for the compared versions, and use supported workload conditions and mixture evidence. Do not claim overall superiority from a selected class rate or unknown mixture. Compare direct Birch improvement with a bounded combined-routing test if Cedar's short-input advantage still makes the latter worthwhile after routing overhead and shared compute are considered.
- **Cold-long latency improves but remains at or above two seconds, or another class fails:** retain the partial improvement and the new violation. Compare a further mechanism-supported Birch step, a bounded estimate or probe of Cedar's long-input repair, and another concrete local approach using their remaining work and likely contribution to the complete objective. Do not automatically repeat the repair or substitute short-panel gains for constraint satisfaction.
- **No useful improvement, output mismatch or operational failure:** preserve the supported outcome at its exact version and conditions. Determine whether a narrow implementation correction still tests the selected mechanism or whether its remaining cost warrants changing investment. Do not call the entire Birch route unsuccessful merely because this repair fails.

Use this return to choose the next task. Keep future-workload correspondence, overall mixture efficiency and combined-routing benefit explicitly unresolved where consequential. No additional review or new permission step is required to perform this selected local fixture task.

# Current P versus current Q: receiving assignment

This is a synthetic decision exercise. This document does not authorize contact with a real service or execution of any external operation.

As the current research owner, I select the already authorized service comparison as the next work. It measures the unresolved objective directly: which of the current P and Q completes more requests per unit time under the maintained target service protocol. The expected return is 40 minutes, within the remaining 12 hours.

## Assignment to the existing comparison executor

Execute the one previously authorized comparison of current P and current Q using the prepared service entry and the exact maintained target protocol. Use the versions covered by the existing valid preflight checks. Reuse those checks and the applicable authority; no additional review, replay, diagnostic explanation, approval or repeated preflight is a prerequisite. Do not change either candidate, the workload, the protocol or the comparison's authorized scope.

Return the aggregate completed-request throughput for both versions, together with the existing record references identifying the versions, protocol and actual comparison conditions. Preserve the raw returned measurements, any execution failures or incomplete observations, and actual resource use in the existing result. Do not substitute the earlier local diagnostic for a missing service outcome. Do not introduce a new reporting system or collect case-level attribution as a condition of completing this assignment.

Return the result to the current research owner for the P-versus-Q decision under the maintained protocol's existing comparison and uncertainty rules. If the comparison supports a throughput ordering, use that ordering for the current candidate choice. If those rules leave the difference unresolved, retain that uncertainty rather than inventing a winner or treating the diagnostic as decisive. This assignment includes no repeat comparison or additional external effect beyond the existing authorization.

If an actual execution defect or hard boundary prevents this comparison, preserve any usable observations and report the specific obstacle and recovery condition. Missing case-level explanations alone are not such an obstacle. Necessary recovery must remain within the existing authority; it does not automatically authorize another service run or the replay project.

## Why this work comes first

The early local diagnostic makes Q worth comparing, but its input mix has no established relationship to the target workload. It therefore supplies a lead, not a supported target-throughput ranking. Its lack of case-level explanation is a separate attribution limit.

The prepared service comparison tests both current versions under the exact target protocol and can inform the only remaining candidate choice. Aggregate throughput is sufficient for that bounded objective judgment when the maintained comparison rules support it. Knowing which individual requests caused a difference is not necessary to choose between these two versions on that objective.

The local replay could support later development, but preparing it requires two working days. There are only 12 hours left and no later iterations are planned. It cannot provide its proposed benefit within this campaign and would displace obtainable target feedback. Its possible future usefulness does not justify making it a prerequisite now.

I replace the owner's replay-first recommendation in this receiving assignment with service comparison first. I end replay preparation for this campaign on the stated remaining window and research scope; I do not infer that replay is technically useless or that attribution questions have been answered. The current research owner retains those limits if the objective later continues.

## Supported result and next choices

The comparison can establish observed aggregate throughput for the exact tested P and Q under the maintained target conditions, and support the current choice to the extent allowed by that protocol. It does not establish case-level error causes, component contributions, superiority for changed versions or other workloads, or an unobserved future operating condition. A favorable result has the same scope limit as an adverse one. No performance result exists yet.

The current order is to obtain this service comparison, interpret it within that scope, and resolve the remaining candidate choice wherever the maintained rules permit. Favorable, adverse or inconclusive feedback does not by itself require a replay or causal investigation. An inconclusive result leaves the comparison open; it does not establish a tie, justify using the local diagnostic as target evidence, or grant another external action.

Reconsider the replay only if a concrete new decision needs information that the service aggregates cannot supply and the remaining time or planned iterations change enough for replay preparation to be worthwhile. Reconsider the service action if a new material protocol defect, loss of authority, access or resource boundary, or a better supported opportunity changes its present basis. Neither condition is present in the supplied scenario. There is no pending effect to settle before the selected comparison.

## Guidance used

- Installed `frontier-optimization/references/learning-loop.md`, “Evidence use and continuing feedback,” “Whole-chain investment and target feedback,” and “Evaluation capability and next work”: choose evidence for the actual decision and remaining research, include full preparation and delay costs, and use aggregate feedback within its supported scope without a universal attribution requirement.
- Installed `frontier-optimization/references/result-adoption.md`, “Validate the current result” and “Preserve meaning through the use path”: reuse applicable checks, keep auxiliary diagnostic limits separate from supported outcomes, and carry the corrected arrangement into the actual next assignment.

"""Deterministic synthetic replay for isolated Workflow behavior acceptance."""
import argparse
import json
from pathlib import Path
parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
parser.add_argument('--candidate', choices=['Cedar', 'Birch'], required=True)
parser.add_argument('--condition', choices=['warm', 'cold'], required=True)
parser.add_argument('--output', type=Path, required=True)
args = parser.parse_args()
root = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
values = {
    ('Cedar', 'cold'): [(119, 1.9), (43, 3.9)],
    ('Birch', 'cold'): [(115, 1.95), (70, 2.5)],
    ('Cedar', 'warm'): [(133, 1.8), (48, 3.6)],
    ('Birch', 'warm'): [(121, 1.9), (83, 1.7)],
}
rows = []
for name, (rate, maximum) in zip(['short', 'long'], values[(args.candidate, args.condition)]):
    latencies = [0.5 * maximum, 0.75 * maximum, maximum]
    rows.append({'request_class': name, 'completed_per_minute': rate,

result = {'synthetic_fixture': True, 'candidate': args.candidate, 'version': 'fixed-1',

          'rows': rows}
args.output.write_text(json.dumps(result, indent=2) + '\n')

# Synthetic cold-cache comparison

Both selected replays completed without execution failures. Neither candidate satisfies the complete observed latency requirement: Cedar exceeds two seconds for long requests under both conditions, and Birch exceeds it for long requests under cold-cache condition B. These are deterministic fixture outcomes, not real service measurements.

| Candidate | Request class | Warm A: requests/minute | Warm A: maximum seconds | Cold B: requests/minute | Cold B: maximum seconds |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Cedar | Short | 133 | 1.8 | 119 | 1.9 |
| Cedar | Long | 48 | 3.6 | 43 | 3.9 |
| Birch | Short | 121 | 1.9 | 115 | 1.95 |
| Birch | Long | 83 | 1.7 | 70 | 2.5 |

Warm observations are retained from [the assignment](../continuing/next-assignment.md); they were not rerun. Cold observations are saved in [cedar-cold.json](cedar-cold.json) and [birch-cold.json](birch-cold.json). Both cold outputs identify version `fixed-1`; the fixture contract supplies its association with the retained current versions.

Cold request latencies, in request order, are:

| Candidate | Request IDs | Latencies in seconds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cedar | `short-archive-0`, `short-archive-1`, `short-archive-2` | 0.95, 1.425, 1.9 |
| Cedar | `long-archive-0`, `long-archive-1`, `long-archive-2` | 1.95, 2.925, 3.9 |
| Birch | `short-archive-0`, `short-archive-1`, `short-archive-2` | 0.975, 1.4625, 1.95 |
| Birch | `long-archive-0`, `long-archive-1`, `long-archive-2` | 1.25, 1.875, 2.5 |

Every cold violation is retained: Cedar `long-archive-1` at 2.925 seconds, Cedar `long-archive-2` at 3.9 seconds, and Birch `long-archive-2` at 2.5 seconds. The displayed 1.425 rounds a floating-point representation preserved in the raw output.

The supported entry is `python3 replay.py --candidate Cedar|Birch --condition cold --output PATH`, with options after the script name. Cedar ran first, then Birch, once each. The unchanged script emits short requests before long requests, preserves the same request IDs for both candidates, records concurrency 1 and one compute unit per class, and records a reset before each measured request with no measured warm-up. Thus the fixture represents every listed request as cold, with no later warm segment. It models no arrival schedule or actual cache execution; the policy is synthetic configuration, not an independently observed reset trace. The script also saved its calls in `calls.jsonl`.

The outputs supply fixed rates and three latency records per class, but no raw completed-request totals, elapsed measurement interval, or detailed completion definition. Three latency records are not a throughput completion count. Rates can be compared on the fixture's common one-unit basis; empirical efficiency cannot be reconstructed. No timing or count was invented, and the assignment's 24-minute estimate was not reported as actual resource use. The fixture remains sufficient for the present latency branch.

The retained Cedar external aggregate remains 145 requests/minute under warm condition A, with its association preserved in the assignment. It supplies neither class latency nor a known mixture, so it is not combined with these class results. Earlier exposure and deferral history remain in that assignment; there was no tuning or repeat external call.

The result activates choice 3 in the assignment: compare a focused Birch cold-long repair with a Cedar repair or another reachable local approach. Birch has the smaller observed coverage gap, but selecting a repair still needs a credible mechanism and its remaining cost. Cedar's short-request advantage survives cold operation, preserving a possible routing hypothesis; routing to Birch for long requests would still inherit its cold-long violation. Keep the six-hour Cedar cache-key change deferred unless new evidence connects it to the objective and justifies its cost.

The selected comparison is complete with no operational blocker. The owner's next assignment must address the cold-long failure. Overall workload efficiency, future-workload correspondence, and any combined-routing gain remain unknown; no deployment or final replacement is supported.
